title: How to use INDEX MATCH in Excel
description: Learn how to use INDEX MATCH in Excel to look up values in any column, search to the left, and build flexible formulas with clear examples.

args.name: return_range
args.text: The range of cells containing the value you want to return.

args.name: lookup_value
args.text: The value or cell reference you want to search for.

args.name: lookup_range
args.text: The single row or column of cells you want to search through.

args.name: match_type
args.text: The match mode. Use 0 for an exact match.

sections.heading: What INDEX MATCH does
sections.text: **INDEX MATCH** pairs two Excel functions to look up values anywhere in a table. `MATCH` searches a row or column and returns the position where it finds a match. `INDEX` then takes that position number and returns the value from another row or column. Unlike `VLOOKUP`, your lookup column can sit anywhere, even to the right of your return data.

sections.heading: A basic lookup example
sections.text: Here is a menu price list for a café. The formula in cell `B6` uses `MATCH` to find Mocha in the drink list, then uses `INDEX` to return its price from the price column.

sections.heading: Look up to the left
sections.text: `VLOOKUP` can only search columns to the right of your lookup value. `INDEX MATCH` does not have this limit. In this kitchen inventory, the item code is in column B and the item name is in column A. The formula in `A6` finds code `K-25` in column B and returns the item name from column A.

sections.heading: Common mistake: mismatched ranges
sections.text: A common mistake is using ranges that start or end on different rows. If your return range is `B2:B5` and your lookup range is `A1:A5`, `MATCH` counts from row 1 while `INDEX` counts from row 2. Every result will be shifted by one row. Always give both ranges the same starting row and length. In addition, always pass `0` as the third argument in `MATCH` to avoid unexpected approximate matches.
